directAnswer: Pope Lando was a Roman cleric who led the Church for roughly seven months, from about July 913 to February 914, during the years when the family of the Roman official Theophylact dominated the city. He is remembered chiefly because his name, Lando, was the last entirely new, non-composite papal name chosen until Pope Francis in 2013.

sections.h2: A Seven-Month Reign in Theophylact's Rome
paras: Lando was elected in the summer of 913, after the short pontificate of Anastasius III. Rome at that moment was effectively governed by the noble Theophylact, his wife Theodora, and their circle, and historians generally assume Lando owed his election to their favor. No surviving source shows him acting independently of that faction.

The papal biographies preserved in the Liber Pontificalis give him only a few lines: his origin, the length of his reign, and his burial. Almost no letters or decrees from his months in office survive, so any claim about his policies would be guesswork. He died in early 914 and was succeeded by the archbishop of Ravenna, who became John X.

sections.h2: Why the Name Lando Still Gets Attention
paras: Before the eleventh century, most popes simply kept their baptismal names, which is why the early lists contain so many one-time names. Lando appears to have done the same. As later popes increasingly adopted the names of honored predecessors, new names disappeared from the list entirely.

That shift makes Lando a footnote of real interest: from 914 until Jorge Mario Bergoglio chose Francis in 2013, no pope took a name that was both new and single. John Paul I, elected in 1978, created a new combination, but it was built from two existing papal names.

keyFacts: Reigned c. July 913 to c. February 914
Personal name Landus; elected after Anastasius III
Served while Theophylact and Theodora dominated Roman politics
Last pope with a new, non-composite name until Francis (2013)
Succeeded by John X, formerly archbishop of Ravenna

faqs.question: Why is Pope Lando connected with Pope Francis?
faqs.answer: Lando is the last pope before Francis to bear a name no earlier pope had used that was not a combination of older names. More than eleven centuries separate the two.

faqs.question: How much is known about Pope Lando's actions as pope?
faqs.answer: Very little. The Liber Pontificalis records only basic details of his short reign, and almost no documents issued in his name survive.

directAnswer: Pope John X (reigned 914–928) was a former archbishop of Ravenna who became one of the most politically active popes of the tenth century. He helped organize the Christian coalition that destroyed the Saracen stronghold on the Garigliano River in 915, crowned Berengar I emperor, and was ultimately deposed and imprisoned by the faction of Marozia, dying in captivity.

sections.h2: From Romagna to the See of Ravenna
paras: John came from Tossignano, near Imola in the Romagna. He served as a deacon at Bologna and was named archbishop of Ravenna, the most important see in northern Italy after Milan, around 905. That experience in a major metropolitan see gave him administrative and political skills that he would bring to Rome.

His transfer from Ravenna to Rome in 914 was unusual at the time, because moving a bishop from one see to another was still viewed with suspicion. The chronicler Liutprand of Cremona, writing decades later and hostile to the Roman nobility, claimed John owed his advancement to Theodora, wife of the powerful Theophylact. Modern historians treat that story with caution, but it is clear that John came to power with the support of the ruling Roman family.

For decades a band of Saracen raiders had held a fortified camp near the mouth of the Garigliano River, between Rome and Naples, from which they plundered the countryside and monasteries such as Monte Cassino. John X made its destruction a priority. He brought together an unusual alliance: Alberic I of Spoleto, the Lombard princes of Capua and Benevento, the coastal cities of Naples and Gaeta, and a Byzantine force.

In 915 the allied army besieged and overran the stronghold, and the pope was present in the field with the troops. The victory removed a threat that had hung over central Italy for a generation and gave the papacy a prestige it had lacked for years. Later that year John crowned Berengar I of Friuli as emperor in Rome.

sections.h2: Croatia, Ravenna and the Wider Church
paras: John's correspondence shows him engaged well beyond Rome. Around 925 he wrote to the Croatian ruler Tomislav and the clergy of Dalmatia about the church synod at Split, pressing for the use of Latin in the liturgy rather than Slavonic and supporting the authority of the archbishop of Split. He also intervened in Frankish church affairs, including the troubled succession to the see of Reims.

After the deaths of Theophylact and Alberic I, power in Rome passed to Marozia, Theophylact's daughter, and her husband Guy, margrave of Tuscany. John sought a counterweight by allying with Hugh of Provence, whom he met at Mantua in 926. The alliance alarmed Marozia's party. In 928 the pope's brother Peter was killed in the Lateran, and John himself was seized and imprisoned.

He died in confinement shortly afterward, probably in 928 or 929. Later writers said he was smothered, though the exact circumstances cannot be confirmed. His fall opened a period in which the papacy was closely controlled by Marozia's family.

keyFacts: Reigned c. March 914 to c. May 928
Born at Tossignano in the Romagna; previously archbishop of Ravenna
Helped lead the coalition that took the Saracen fortress on the Garigliano (915)
Crowned Berengar I emperor in 915
Deposed and imprisoned by Marozia's faction; died in captivity

faqs.question: Did Pope John X really fight in a battle?
faqs.answer: Contemporary and near-contemporary sources place him with the allied army at the Garigliano in 915. He accompanied the forces that besieged and destroyed the Saracen camp, which was unusual for a pope.

faqs.question: Why was Pope John X deposed?
faqs.answer: His alliance with Hugh of Provence threatened the power of Marozia and her husband Guy of Tuscany, who controlled Rome. They had him arrested in 928, and he died in prison.

faqs.question: What did John X decide about the Slavonic liturgy in Croatia?
faqs.answer: In letters connected with the synod of Split around 925, he urged the Croatian clergy to celebrate the liturgy in Latin and discouraged the spread of Slavonic worship.

directAnswer: Pope Leo VI reigned for only about seven months, from May 928 to early 929, after John X had been imprisoned by Marozia's party. He was a Roman priest whose short pontificate left few records beyond a ruling on church affairs in Dalmatia.

sections.h2: Elected While His Predecessor Was Still Alive
paras: Leo VI was chosen in May 928, while John X was still held captive. That circumstance alone shows who controlled papal elections at the time: Marozia and her husband Guy of Tuscany. The Liber Pontificalis identifies Leo as a Roman, the son of a man named Christopher who held the office of primicerius in the papal administration.
Whether Leo approved of the treatment of his predecessor is not recorded. His reign lasted only until about February 929.

sections.h2: A Ruling for the Church in Dalmatia
paras: One act of his short reign is reasonably well attested. Following the synods held at Split, Leo confirmed the reorganization of the Dalmatian church under the archbishop of Split and instructed Bishop Gregory of Nin, whose see had been downgraded, to accept the decision and confine himself to his diocese. The ruling continued the line John X had taken.
Beyond this, nothing substantial is known of his policies. He was buried in St. Peter's Basilica and was followed by Stephen VII.

keyFacts: Reigned c. May 928 to c. February 929
Roman by birth; son of Christopher, a papal official
Elected while John X was imprisoned by Marozia's faction
Confirmed the Split synod's arrangements for the Dalmatian church
Buried in St. Peter's Basilica

faqs.question: Why was Leo VI elected while John X was still alive?
faqs.answer: John X had been deposed and imprisoned by Marozia and Guy of Tuscany, who controlled Rome. They arranged the election of a successor without waiting for John's death.

faqs.question: What is Leo VI known for?
faqs.answer: His main recorded act is confirming the decisions of the synods of Split, which placed the Dalmatian bishops under the archbishop of Split and limited the bishop of Nin.

directAnswer: Pope Stephen VII, sometimes numbered Stephen VIII, reigned from 929 to 931 in a Rome dominated by Marozia. Little is known of him beyond his Roman origin and a handful of privileges granted to monasteries.

paras: Stephen was a Roman, described in the papal records as the son of Theodemund. He was elected in early 929 and is generally regarded by historians as a candidate acceptable to Marozia, who at this point governed the city and was preparing the way for her own son to take the papal throne.

The surviving documents from his two years consist mainly of grants and confirmations of privileges for religious houses in France and Italy. These were routine acts, but they show that the papal chancery kept working even under strong lay control.
Stephen died in March 931. His successor was John XI, Marozia's son, a choice that underlines how fully the papacy had fallen under the influence of her family.

The two numbers attached to this pope come from an eighth-century problem. A priest named Stephen was elected in 752 but died before being consecrated. Older lists counted him, later ones did not, so every subsequent Pope Stephen carries two possible numbers. The Vatican's current practice counts the man elected in 752 only parenthetically, which produces the double numbering seen here.

keyFacts: Reigned c. February 929 to March 931
Roman by birth; son of Theodemund
Generally considered a nominee of Marozia
Granted privileges to monasteries in France and Italy
Also numbered Stephen VIII because of the disputed Stephen of 752

faqs.question: Why is Stephen VII sometimes called Stephen VIII?
faqs.answer: A Stephen elected in 752 died before consecration. Whether to count him changes the number of every later Pope Stephen, including this one.

faqs.question: Who succeeded Stephen VII?
faqs.answer: He was followed in 931 by John XI, the son of Marozia, who then dominated Roman politics.

directAnswer: Pope John XI (reigned 931–935) was the son of Marozia, the dominant figure in Roman politics, and became pope as a young man. After his half-brother Alberic II seized power in 932, John was confined to the Lateran and allowed only spiritual functions, though he did grant an important privilege to the abbey of Cluny.

sections.h2: Marozia's Son on the Papal Throne
paras: John was elected in March 931, probably in his early twenties. His mother Marozia controlled Rome, and his election was her doing. The question of his father has long been debated: Liutprand of Cremona and the Liber Pontificalis indicate that he was the son of Pope Sergius III, while others have identified his father as Marozia's first husband, Alberic I of Spoleto. Most historians accept the earlier sources' account, though certainty is impossible.
In 932 Marozia married Hugh of Provence, by then king of Italy, a match many considered uncanonical because Hugh was the half-brother of her late husband Guy.

sections.h2: Alberic II and the Confined Pope
paras: The marriage provoked a revolt. Marozia's son Alberic II, angered by Hugh's presence, raised the Roman people against him in 932. Hugh fled, Marozia was imprisoned, and Alberic took control of the city as its prince and senator. He kept his half-brother John under close supervision at the Lateran.

From then on, according to the sources, John exercised only his sacramental and spiritual duties, while Alberic handled all temporal affairs, including appointments and diplomacy. This arrangement shaped papal elections for the next two decades.

Two of John's acts had lasting effects. In 931 he issued a privilege to the abbey of Cluny confirming its independence and allowing it to receive monks from other houses seeking reform, which helped Cluny spread its influence. In 933 papal legates attended the consecration of Theophylact, son of the Byzantine emperor Romanos I, as patriarch of Constantinople, a sign that communication with the East continued. John died around December 935.

keyFacts: Reigned c. March 931 to c. December 935
Son of Marozia; early sources name Sergius III as his father
Confined to the Lateran by his half-brother Alberic II from 932
Granted a key privilege to the abbey of Cluny in 931
Sent legates to the consecration of Patriarch Theophylact of Constantinople (933)

faqs.question: Was John XI really the son of a pope?
faqs.answer: Liutprand of Cremona and the Liber Pontificalis say his father was Sergius III. Some writers prefer Alberic I of Spoleto, but most historians follow the early sources.

faqs.question: Why did John XI have so little power?
faqs.answer: After 932 his half-brother Alberic II ruled Rome and limited John to purely spiritual functions, keeping political decisions for himself.

faqs.question: What did John XI do for Cluny?
faqs.answer: His 931 privilege confirmed the abbey's freedom and allowed it to accept monks from other monasteries, helping the Cluniac reform movement expand.

directAnswer: Pope Leo VII reigned from January 936 to July 939 under the control of Alberic II, the ruler of Rome. He is best known for supporting monastic reform, inviting Odo of Cluny to Rome, and naming Archbishop Frederick of Mainz as his vicar in Germany.

paras: Leo VII was elected in January 936, apparently with Alberic II's approval. Later tradition describes him as a monk, and he is sometimes listed as a Benedictine, though the early sources say little about his background. His reign fell entirely within the period of Alberic's rule, and he seems to have accepted that his role would be primarily religious.

sections.h2: Odo of Cluny and Monastic Reform
paras: Leo's most notable contribution was his support for monastic renewal. Abbot Odo of Cluny came to Rome during his reign, both to help negotiate peace between Alberic and Hugh of Provence and to reform monasteries in and around the city. With papal support and Alberic's cooperation, Odo worked to restore discipline in Roman houses, including St. Paul Outside the Walls.
Leo also issued privileges to Cluny and other reformed monasteries, encouraging the spread of a movement that would shape Western monasticism for the next two centuries.

sections.h2: A Vicar for the German Church
paras: Leo appointed Frederick, archbishop of Mainz, as his vicar and legate in Germany, giving him authority to address church discipline there. In correspondence with Frederick, the pope addressed several pastoral questions, including the treatment of Jews who refused baptism; he rejected forced conversion while permitting their expulsion, a ruling that reflects the harsh assumptions of the age. Leo died in July 939.

keyFacts: Reigned 3 January 936 to 13 July 939
Elected under the rule of Alberic II
Supported Odo of Cluny's reform of Roman monasteries
Named Archbishop Frederick of Mainz papal vicar in Germany
Traditionally described as a Benedictine monk

faqs.question: How did Leo VII support Cluny?
faqs.answer: He welcomed Abbot Odo of Cluny to Rome, backed his reform of Roman monasteries, and granted privileges to Cluniac houses.

faqs.question: Who really governed Rome during Leo VII's reign?
faqs.answer: Alberic II, prince and senator of the Romans, controlled the city's political affairs while the pope focused on church matters.

directAnswer: Pope Stephen VIII, sometimes numbered Stephen IX, reigned from 939 to 942 while Alberic II ruled Rome. Reportedly born in East Francia, he is best remembered for supporting the West Frankish king Louis IV against rebellious nobles.

sections.h2: A Pope of Possible German Birth
paras: Several sources describe Stephen as having been born in East Francia, the German kingdom, though he spent his career as a cleric in Rome. He was elected in July 939, presumably with Alberic II's consent, and like his immediate predecessors he exercised little political authority in the city itself.

sections.h2: Intervening for Louis IV of France
paras: His most notable act concerned the West Frankish kingdom. King Louis IV, known as d'Outremer, faced opposition from powerful nobles, including Hugh the Great. In 942 Stephen sent a legate to Francia instructing the nobles to recognize Louis and threatening excommunication against those who continued in revolt. The intervention gave Louis valuable support during a fragile period.

Stephen died around late October 942. Some later medieval writers, notably Martin of Opava, claimed he was mutilated during a conspiracy, but this story appears long after the fact and is not confirmed by earlier sources. Historians generally regard it as doubtful. As with the earlier Stephens, his number varies depending on whether the Stephen elected in 752 is counted.

keyFacts: Reigned 14 July 939 to c. 30 October 942
Reportedly born in East Francia
Served under the political control of Alberic II
Backed King Louis IV of West Francia, threatening rebel nobles with excommunication (942)
Also numbered Stephen IX

faqs.question: How did Stephen VIII help King Louis IV?
faqs.answer: He sent a legate ordering the Frankish nobles to submit to Louis IV and threatened excommunication against those who refused.

faqs.question: Was Stephen VIII mutilated?
faqs.answer: A late medieval account says so, but earlier sources do not, and historians treat the story as unreliable.

directAnswer: Pope Marinus II reigned from 942 to 946, chosen under the authority of Alberic II, the lay ruler of Rome. His pontificate was quiet and focused on church administration; medieval scribes later confused his name, listing him as Martin III.

paras: Marinus was a Roman cleric elected in late October 942. Like the popes immediately before him, he owed his election to Alberic II, who controlled every appointment of consequence in Rome. The sources suggest he accepted this arrangement and did not attempt to challenge Alberic's authority in civil matters.

The documents from his reign concern privileges for monasteries and churches, including grants supporting the reform movement that Alberic and Odo of Cluny had encouraged in Rome. He also dealt with ordinary questions of church discipline. Nothing dramatic is recorded of his three and a half years, and the Liber Pontificalis offers only brief notes. He died in the spring of 946.

Medieval copyists sometimes read the abbreviated names of Marinus I and Marinus II as Martin, and the two popes were listed as Martin II and Martin III. When Simon de Brion became pope in 1281, he took the name Martin IV, accepting that faulty count. In reality only one earlier pope, Martin I, had borne the name.

keyFacts: Reigned 30 October 942 to c. May 946
Roman cleric elected under Alberic II
Granted privileges to monasteries and churches
Misidentified in medieval lists as Martin III
The error explains why the 1281 pope became Martin IV

faqs.question: Why was Marinus II called Martin III?
faqs.answer: Medieval scribes misread the names of Marinus I and II as Martin, so both were mistakenly counted among the popes named Martin.

faqs.question: Did Marinus II have political power in Rome?
faqs.answer: No. Alberic II controlled Rome's government, and Marinus confined himself largely to church administration.

directAnswer: Pope Agapetus II reigned from 946 to 955, the longest pontificate of Alberic II's era. He settled the disputed see of Reims through his legate at the Synod of Ingelheim, declined to crown Otto I emperor under Alberic's pressure, and saw Alberic arrange for his own son to succeed as pope.

sections.h2: A Long Reign Under Alberic II
paras: Agapetus was a Roman, elected in May 946. Over nearly ten years he worked within the boundaries Alberic II set, but his reign was more active than those of his immediate predecessors, especially in relations with the churches north of the Alps. He also continued to support monastic reform in Rome.

sections.h2: The Synod of Ingelheim and the See of Reims
paras: For years two rival claimants, Artold and Hugh of Vermandois, fought over the archdiocese of Reims, a dispute tangled up with the conflict between King Louis IV and his nobles. In 948 Agapetus sent his legate, Bishop Marinus, to a synod at Ingelheim attended by Otto I and Louis IV. The synod upheld Artold and excommunicated Hugh, and later Roman synods confirmed the decision.

sections.h2: Otto I and the Oath for Octavian
paras: When Otto I asked to come to Rome for imperial coronation around 951–952, Agapetus declined. Alberic, who had no wish to see a powerful emperor in the city, is generally assumed to have been behind the refusal. Shortly before his death in 954, Alberic had the Roman nobles swear to elect his son Octavian as the next pope. When Agapetus died in November 955, that oath was carried out, and Octavian became John XII.

keyFacts: Reigned 10 May 946 to 8 November 955
Roman by birth; pope under Alberic II
His legate presided at the Synod of Ingelheim (948), which settled the Reims dispute
Declined Otto I's request for imperial coronation
Succeeded by Alberic's son Octavian, who became John XII

faqs.question: Why didn't Agapetus II crown Otto I?
faqs.answer: Alberic II opposed the presence of a strong emperor in Rome, and the pope declined Otto's request, almost certainly at Alberic's urging.

faqs.question: What was decided at the Synod of Ingelheim?
faqs.answer: The synod, led by the papal legate, recognized Artold as archbishop of Reims and excommunicated his rival Hugh of Vermandois.

directAnswer: Pope John XII (reigned 955–964), born Octavian, was the son of Alberic II and became pope as a young man of about eighteen. He crowned Otto I as emperor in 962, a turning point in European history, but soon broke with him, was deposed by an imperial synod in 963, and died in 964 after briefly regaining Rome.

paras: Octavian was born into the family that had ruled Rome for half a century. His father, Alberic II, made the Roman nobility swear to elect him pope, and in December 955 he succeeded Agapetus II while also inheriting his father's civil authority. He was very young, and contemporaries, especially the hostile chronicler Liutprand of Cremona, portrayed him as unsuited to the office.

Liutprand's account, written for Otto's court, contains many accusations of personal misconduct. Historians accept that John's conduct gave serious grounds for criticism while recognizing that the most lurid details come from a partisan source.

sections.h2: The Coronation of Otto I in 962
paras: John's position grew dangerous when Berengar II, king of Italy, pressed on papal territory. The pope turned to Otto I of Germany for help. Otto came to Rome, and on 2 February 962 John crowned him and his wife Adelaide in St. Peter's. The event is often regarded as the beginning of what later became known as the Holy Roman Empire.

Days later Otto issued the document known as the Diploma Ottonianum, confirming the papacy's territorial possessions while asserting imperial rights, including a role in the oversight of papal elections. Around the same time John authorized the creation of an archdiocese at Magdeburg to organize missions among the Slavs.

The alliance did not last. Fearing Otto's dominance, John opened negotiations with Berengar's son Adalbert and with other powers. Otto returned to Rome in 963, and John fled. A synod convened under Otto's authority in November 963 heard accusations against the pope and, when he refused to appear, declared him deposed. The synod then elected a layman, who became Leo VIII.
The legitimacy of deposing a pope in this way was questionable even at the time, and the episode remains one of the most debated in papal history.

Once Otto left Rome, John returned in early 964. He held a synod that annulled the decisions against him and punished some of his opponents. He died on 14 May 964, outside Rome, while still in his twenties. Liutprand gives a scandalous account of his death, but the true circumstances are not known with certainty. Historians mark his death as the close of the so-called saeculum obscurum, the period of noble domination of the papacy.

keyFacts: Reigned 16 December 955 to 14 May 964
Born Octavian, son of Alberic II; elected at about eighteen
Crowned Otto I emperor on 2 February 962
Diploma Ottonianum issued in 962
Deposed by a synod under Otto in 963; returned to Rome in 964
Authorized the archdiocese of Magdeburg

faqs.question: Why is John XII's coronation of Otto I important?
faqs.answer: It renewed the Western imperial title in Germany and is commonly seen as the start of the Holy Roman Empire, binding papal and imperial politics together for centuries.

faqs.question: Was John XII validly deposed?
faqs.answer: A synod summoned by Otto I declared him deposed in 963, but the procedure was irregular and contested. John reversed it after returning to Rome, and his status remains a matter of historical debate.

faqs.question: How reliable are the accusations against John XII?
faqs.answer: Many come from Liutprand of Cremona, a writer loyal to Otto I. Historians take his charges seriously but recognize his strong bias.

directAnswer: Pope Benedict V reigned for only about a month in 964. Elected by the Romans after the death of John XII in opposition to Emperor Otto I's candidate Leo VIII, he was deposed when Otto took Rome, and he died in exile in Hamburg.

paras: Benedict was a Roman deacon admired for his learning, which earned him the nickname Grammaticus. After John XII died in May 964, the Romans refused to accept Leo VIII, whom Otto I had installed the year before, and elected Benedict instead. They hoped the emperor would accept their choice.

Otto did not. He besieged Rome, and famine soon forced the city to surrender. In June 964 a synod in the Lateran, held in the emperor's presence, deposed Benedict. According to the sources he accepted the judgment, and the insignia of his office were removed. He was reduced to the rank of deacon.

Otto sent him north into the custody of Adaldag, archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen, who treated him with respect. Benedict died in Hamburg, probably in 965. The chronicler Thietmar of Merseburg reports that his remains were later returned to Rome. The modern Church counts both Benedict and Leo VIII in its list of popes, although the legitimacy of each has been debated.

keyFacts: Reigned 22 May 964 to 23 June 964
Known as Benedict the Grammarian for his learning
Elected by the Romans against Otto I's candidate Leo VIII
Deposed at a Lateran synod in Otto's presence
Died in exile in Hamburg, probably 965

faqs.question: Why was Benedict V deposed?
faqs.answer: Emperor Otto I regarded Leo VIII as the rightful pope and refused to accept the Romans' election of Benedict. After besieging Rome, he had a synod depose him.

faqs.question: Where did Benedict V die?
faqs.answer: He died in exile at Hamburg, where Archbishop Adaldag had custody of him.

directAnswer: Pope Leo VIII was a Roman layman elected in 963 at the synod that Otto I convened to depose John XII. His pontificate was contested until Benedict V's deposition in June 964, and the modern Church counts him as legitimate from that point until his death in 965.

paras: Leo was a senior official of the papal administration, holding the post of protoscriniarius, head of the chancery's scribes, but he was not a cleric. After Otto's synod declared John XII deposed in December 963, it chose Leo, and he received all the clerical orders within a very short time before being consecrated. Such rapid elevation violated church norms and fueled opposition to him.

When Otto left Rome in early 964, the Romans rose against Leo, and he fled to the emperor. John XII returned and condemned him. After John's death the Romans elected Benedict V, but Otto besieged the city, restored Leo, and had Benedict deposed in June 964. From then until his death on 1 March 965, Leo reigned without a rival.

Several documents attributed to Leo VIII grant the emperor sweeping rights, including control over papal elections and the investiture of bishops. Historians recognize these as forgeries produced during the eleventh-century Investiture Controversy. Leo's actual surviving acts are few, and his reign is best understood as a product of imperial politics.

keyFacts: Elected December 963; counted as legitimate pope from 23 June 964 to 1 March 965
A layman and papal official (protoscriniarius) before election
Received all clerical orders in rapid succession
Restored by Otto I after the deposition of Benedict V
Imperial privileges bearing his name are later forgeries

faqs.question: Why is Leo VIII's legitimacy debated?
faqs.answer: He was elected while John XII was still alive, through a deposition of questionable validity. The Church counts him as pope only after Benedict V's deposition in 964.

faqs.question: Did Leo VIII give the emperor control over papal elections?
faqs.answer: Documents claiming so exist, but they are later forgeries from the Investiture Controversy, not genuine acts of Leo.

directAnswer: Pope John XIII (reigned 965–972) was bishop of Narni before his election with the support of Emperor Otto I. Driven out of Rome by a revolt and then restored, he crowned Otto II co-emperor, crowned the Byzantine princess Theophanu, and organized the archdiocese of Magdeburg to anchor the Church among the Slavs.

sections.h2: Bishop of Narni and Imperial Ally
paras: John was a Roman cleric, reportedly connected to a prominent Roman family, who served at the papal court before becoming bishop of Narni. After the death of Leo VIII, he was elected on 1 October 965 with the approval of imperial representatives. His close association with Otto I made him unpopular with many Roman nobles who resented imperial influence.

Within weeks, in December 965, a faction of Roman aristocrats seized the pope and imprisoned him in the Castel Sant'Angelo before sending him out of the city. He escaped and found refuge at Capua with Prince Pandulf Ironhead, whose city he rewarded by raising it to the rank of an archbishopric.

Otto I marched south in 966. The Romans, anticipating his anger, allowed John back in November 966. Otto punished the ringleaders of the revolt severely, and the pope remained closely aligned with the emperor for the rest of his reign.

At Christmas 967 John crowned Otto's son, Otto II, as co-emperor in St. Peter's, securing the dynasty's succession. Five years later, on 14 April 972, he married Otto II to Theophanu, a Byzantine princess, and crowned her empress. The marriage linked the Ottonian court to Constantinople and brought Byzantine culture and art into the West.

John XII had authorized an archdiocese at Magdeburg in 962, but organizing it took years of negotiation with German bishops whose territory would be affected. In 968 John XIII completed the arrangement, and Adalbert, a former missionary to the Rus', became the first archbishop of Magdeburg with suffragan sees along the Slavic frontier. The new province became a base for missionary work east of the Elbe.
John also supported monastic reform and confirmed privileges for many religious houses. He died on 6 September 972, and chroniclers after his death referred to him as "the Good."

keyFacts: Reigned 1 October 965 to 6 September 972
Previously bishop of Narni
Expelled by Roman nobles in 965; restored with Otto I's support in 966
Crowned Otto II co-emperor at Christmas 967
Crowned Theophanu empress at her marriage to Otto II (972)
Organized the archdiocese of Magdeburg (968)

faqs.question: Why was Pope John XIII imprisoned soon after his election?
faqs.answer: Roman nobles opposed to Otto I's influence saw him as the emperor's man. They seized him in December 965, though he escaped and was restored the next year.

faqs.question: What role did John XIII play in the marriage of Otto II and Theophanu?
faqs.answer: He performed their marriage in Rome in April 972 and crowned Theophanu empress, sealing an alliance between the Ottonian and Byzantine courts.

faqs.question: Why was Magdeburg important to John XIII?
faqs.answer: Magdeburg became an archdiocese under him in 968, organizing the Church along the Slavic frontier and supporting missionary work in the East.

directAnswer: Pope Benedict VI reigned from January 973 to June 974. A Roman elected with Otto I's approval, he lost his protection when Otto died and was imprisoned and killed by a Roman faction that installed the antipope Boniface VII.

paras: Benedict was a Roman, the son of a man named Hildebrand, and served as a cardinal-deacon before his election. He was chosen after the death of John XIII, but his consecration on 19 January 973 had to wait until Otto I gave his approval, which shows how much the emperor's consent counted after 962.

sections.h2: The Death of Otto I and a Roman Revolt
paras: Otto I died in May 973, and his son Otto II was occupied with affairs in Germany. Roman nobles hostile to imperial influence, led by Crescentius, a member of the family that would dominate Rome for decades, seized the opportunity. In June 974 they imprisoned Benedict in the Castel Sant'Angelo and raised the deacon Franco to the papal throne as Boniface VII, now listed as an antipope.

When an imperial envoy arrived to demand Benedict's release, his captors had him strangled in prison. The Liber Pontificalis names a priest called Stephen as the killer, acting on Franco's orders. Little else about Benedict's personal outlook or reign is recorded; his death is the most documented fact of his life.

keyFacts: Reigned 19 January 973 to c. June 974
Roman by birth; son of Hildebrand
Consecrated only after Otto I approved his election
Imprisoned in the Castel Sant'Angelo by Crescentius's faction
Killed in prison; antipope Boniface VII was installed

faqs.question: Who killed Pope Benedict VI?
faqs.answer: According to the Liber Pontificalis, a priest named Stephen strangled him in prison on the orders of Franco, who had been set up as the antipope Boniface VII.

faqs.question: Why was Benedict VI vulnerable after 973?
faqs.answer: His protector, Otto I, died in 973, and the new emperor was far away, leaving Roman nobles free to move against the pope.

directAnswer: Pope Benedict VII reigned from 974 to 983, bringing a decade of relative stability after the murder of Benedict VI. A former bishop of Sutri chosen with imperial backing, he resisted the antipope Boniface VII, condemned simony, and supported monastic reform.

sections.h2: The Bishop of Sutri Takes Office
paras: Benedict was bishop of Sutri, north of Rome, and was related to the family of Alberic II. He was elected in October 974 with the support of the imperial representative, Count Sicco, after the antipope Boniface VII had fled Rome. Boniface escaped to Constantinople with treasure taken from the Vatican.

Boniface returned to Rome around 980, and Benedict was forced to leave the city. Emperor Otto II came to Italy and restored him in 981. The pope and the emperor then held a synod in Rome at which, among other matters, the diocese of Merseburg was suppressed at the emperor's wish, a decision later reversed.

Benedict held a synod in 981 that condemned simony, the buying and selling of church offices, which was widespread at the time. He supported reformed monasteries, granting privileges to communities such as Cluny, and encouraged monastic life in Rome. He died on 10 July 983 and was buried in the basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.

keyFacts: Reigned c. October 974 to 10 July 983
Previously bishop of Sutri; related to Alberic II's family
Elected with the support of imperial envoy Count Sicco
Temporarily expelled by antipope Boniface VII; restored by Otto II in 981
Held a synod condemning simony (981)

faqs.question: How did Benedict VII deal with the antipope Boniface VII?
faqs.answer: Boniface fled when Benedict was elected, returned around 980, and briefly drove him out. Otto II restored Benedict in 981.

faqs.question: Where is Benedict VII buried?
faqs.answer: He was buried in the Roman basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.

directAnswer: Pope John XIV, born Pietro Canepanova, was bishop of Pavia and imperial chancellor for Italy before Emperor Otto II arranged his election in late 983. After Otto's sudden death, the antipope Boniface VII returned, imprisoned John in the Castel Sant'Angelo, and he died there in August 984.

sections.h2: Otto II's Chancellor and Bishop of Pavia
paras: Pietro Canepanova came from Pavia, the old Lombard capital, and served as its bishop. He was also Otto II's archchancellor for Italy, one of the emperor's most trusted administrators. When Benedict VII died in 983, Otto, then in Rome, secured Pietro's election. He took the name John, by most accounts out of reluctance to bear the name of the apostle Peter as pope.
Because he was chosen by the emperor rather than through the usual Roman process, the local nobility regarded him as an outsider.

Within weeks of John's election, Otto II died in Rome on 7 December 983, still in his twenties. The emperor was buried in the atrium of St. Peter's. The heir, Otto III, was a small child in Germany, leaving the pope without effective support in a hostile city.

In April 984 the antipope Boniface VII, who had been in Constantinople since his flight a decade earlier, came back to Rome with the help of local allies. He had John seized and imprisoned in the Castel Sant'Angelo. John died there on 20 August 984, according to the sources either from starvation or by poison. Boniface held the city until his own death the following year.

keyFacts: Reigned c. December 983 to 20 August 984
Born Pietro Canepanova in Pavia; bishop of Pavia
Archchancellor of Italy under Emperor Otto II
Chose the name John rather than reign as Peter
Imprisoned by antipope Boniface VII; died in the Castel Sant'Angelo

faqs.question: Why didn't Pope John XIV keep his baptismal name?
faqs.answer: His name was Peter, and he chose John instead, by most accounts out of reverence for St. Peter, whose name no pope had taken as a papal name.

faqs.question: How did John XIV die?
faqs.answer: He was imprisoned by the antipope Boniface VII and died in the Castel Sant'Angelo in August 984, reportedly of starvation or poison.

directAnswer: Pope John XV (reigned 985–996) is remembered as the first pope to canonize a saint through a formal papal act, declaring Ulrich of Augsburg a saint in 993. He also mediated peace between England and Normandy, though in Rome his authority was limited by the noble Crescentius II.

sections.h2: A Roman Priest in the Shadow of the Crescentii
paras: John was a Roman, the son of a priest named Leo, and was himself a priest at the time of his election in 985, after the death of the antipope Boniface VII. Real power in the city belonged to the Crescentii family, especially Crescentius II, who held the title of patrician. Chroniclers accused the pope of nepotism and greed, though their accounts are not free of bias.
Despite these limits, John's pontificate of more than ten years was one of the most significant of the late tenth century, largely because of his activity beyond Rome.

sections.h2: The Canonization of Ulrich of Augsburg
paras: Before John XV, saints were generally recognized through local veneration approved by a bishop. At a Lateran synod in 993, John formally declared Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg (died 973), a saint, after hearing an account of his life and miracles. The papal bull that followed is the earliest surviving document in which a pope canonizes someone.

The step did not immediately end local canonizations, but it set a precedent. Over the following centuries the papacy gradually reserved canonization to itself, a principle firmly established by the thirteenth century.

In 991 John sent his legate, Bishop Leo of Trevi, to England and Normandy to settle a conflict between King Æthelred of England and Duke Richard I of Normandy. The resulting treaty, in which each side promised not to shelter the other's enemies, is one of the earliest papal-brokered agreements between Western rulers.

sections.h2: The Reims Dispute and the Final Crisis
paras: John was drawn into a long conflict over the archdiocese of Reims. In 991 a French synod deposed Archbishop Arnulf and elected the scholar Gerbert of Aurillac in his place without papal consent. John objected to the procedure, and his legates pressed for Arnulf's restoration, a case finally settled under his successor.

By 995 tensions with Crescentius II forced John to leave Rome for Tuscany, and he appealed to the young King Otto III for help. Crescentius allowed him to return, but John died in early 996, before Otto reached Rome.

keyFacts: Reigned c. August 985 to c. March 996
First formal papal canonization: Ulrich of Augsburg, 993
His legate mediated a 991 treaty between Æthelred of England and Richard I of Normandy
Opposed the deposition of Archbishop Arnulf of Reims
His Roman authority was constrained by the patrician Crescentius II

faqs.question: Who was the first saint formally canonized by a pope?
faqs.answer: Ulrich of Augsburg, canonized by John XV at a Lateran synod in 993. The papal bull is the oldest known record of a papal canonization.

faqs.question: What was John XV's role in English history?
faqs.answer: He sent a legate who negotiated a peace treaty in 991 between King Æthelred of England and Duke Richard I of Normandy.

faqs.question: Why did John XV leave Rome in 995?
faqs.answer: Conflict with Crescentius II, who dominated Rome's government, led him to withdraw to Tuscany and ask Otto III for help.

directAnswer: Pope Gregory V (reigned 996–999), born Bruno of Carinthia, was a cousin of Emperor Otto III and is generally counted as the first German pope. He crowned Otto emperor in 996, was driven from Rome by Crescentius II and an antipope, and was restored by Otto in 998 before dying in 999 at about twenty-seven.

sections.h2: Bruno of Carinthia, the Emperor's Cousin
paras: Bruno was the son of Otto, duke of Carinthia, and a great-grandson of Otto I, making him a cousin of the young King Otto III. He served as a chaplain in the royal household. When the news of John XV's death reached Otto III, who was on his way to Rome in 996, the king nominated Bruno, then about twenty-four, and the Romans accepted him.

Bruno chose the name Gregory, recalling Gregory the Great. His election marked a deliberate break: for the first time in centuries, the pope was a non-Italian chosen for his connection to the imperial court rather than Roman family politics.

On 21 May 996 Gregory crowned Otto III emperor in St. Peter's. The two young men shared hopes of reforming the Church and renewing the Christian empire. Gregory showed clemency at first, persuading Otto to pardon Crescentius II rather than exile him, a decision that would soon backfire.

sections.h2: Crescentius II and the Antipope John XVI
paras: After Otto returned to Germany, Crescentius rose against the pope, and by 997 Gregory had been forced out of Rome. Crescentius installed John Philagathos, archbishop of Piacenza and formerly a tutor of Otto, as the antipope John XVI. From northern Italy Gregory held a synod at Pavia in 997 that excommunicated Crescentius.

Otto came back in early 998 and retook the city. Crescentius was executed, and Philagathos was mutilated and humiliated, treatment that drew a public protest from the elderly monk St. Nilus of Rossano.

Gregory took a firm line in French church affairs. He insisted on the restoration of Archbishop Arnulf to Reims, reversing the deposition that John XV had opposed. He also ordered King Robert II of France to separate from his wife Bertha of Burgundy because their marriage fell within forbidden degrees of kinship, imposing penance on the couple.
Gregory died suddenly in February 999 and was buried in St. Peter's, where his sarcophagus can still be seen in the Vatican grottoes.

keyFacts: Reigned 3 May 996 to 18 February 999
Born Bruno of Carinthia; cousin of Otto III
Generally regarded as the first German pope
Crowned Otto III emperor on 21 May 996
Opposed by Crescentius II and the antipope John XVI
Buried in St. Peter's; his sarcophagus survives in the Vatican grottoes

faqs.question: Why is Gregory V called the first German pope?
faqs.answer: He was a member of the Saxon imperial dynasty, born in the German lands, and was nominated by his cousin Otto III. No earlier pope is reliably identified as German.

faqs.question: Who was the antipope during Gregory V's reign?
faqs.answer: John Philagathos, installed by Crescentius II in 997 as John XVI. He was deposed and mutilated when Otto III retook Rome in 998.

faqs.question: Why did Gregory V intervene in King Robert II's marriage?
faqs.answer: Robert's marriage to Bertha of Burgundy was within the degrees of kinship forbidden by church law, so the pope ordered them to separate.

directAnswer: Pope Sylvester II (reigned 999–1003), born Gerbert of Aurillac, was the first French pope and among the most learned men of his age. A teacher of mathematics, astronomy and logic, he worked closely with Emperor Otto III and helped establish independent church provinces in Poland and Hungary.

sections.h2: Gerbert of Aurillac, Scholar and Teacher
paras: Gerbert was born around 946 in the Auvergne in south-central France, of humble family, and entered the Benedictine monastery of Saint-Géraud at Aurillac. Around 967 he went to Catalonia, where he studied mathematics in the region of Vic and Ripoll. There he encountered learning that had come from the Islamic world, including Arabic numerals and astronomical instruments.

As master of the cathedral school of Reims, he became famous for his teaching. He used an abacus with numbered counters, worked with the astrolabe and armillary spheres, and taught logic, rhetoric and classical authors. His letters, which survive in a large collection, show a sharp mind deeply involved in the politics of his time.

Otto II named Gerbert abbot of the monastery of Bobbio in northern Italy in 982, but local opposition made his position difficult. In 991 he was elected archbishop of Reims after the deposition of Arnulf, but the papacy refused to accept the procedure, and the dispute eventually cost him the see.

Otto III, who had been his pupil, brought him into the imperial circle and in 998 secured his appointment as archbishop of Ravenna. A year later, after the death of Gregory V, Otto supported his election as pope.

sections.h2: Why He Chose the Name Sylvester
paras: Gerbert took the name Sylvester, recalling Sylvester I, the pope of Emperor Constantine's era. The choice expressed the ideal he and Otto shared: a close partnership between pope and emperor at the head of a renewed Christian world. Otto's residence in Rome and his program of imperial renewal gave that ideal visible form.

sections.h2: Poland, Hungary and the Shape of Christian Europe
paras: Sylvester's pontificate had lasting consequences for Central Europe. In 1000 he approved the creation of an archdiocese at Gniezno in Poland, built around the tomb of the martyr St. Adalbert of Prague, giving the Polish church its own metropolitan. Around the same time an archdiocese was established at Esztergom for Hungary. Tradition holds that Sylvester sent a royal crown to Stephen of Hungary, who was crowned in 1000 or 1001, though the history of the surviving Holy Crown is more complex.

In 1001 a revolt in Rome forced both Otto and Sylvester out of the city. After Otto's death in early 1002, Sylvester returned and lived quietly until his death on 12 May 1003. He was buried in St. John Lateran. Legends portraying him as a sorcerer arose later, especially from the twelfth century onward; they reflect suspicion of his scientific learning rather than historical fact.

keyFacts: Reigned 2 April 999 to 12 May 1003
Born Gerbert of Aurillac in the Auvergne, c. 946; Benedictine monk
First French pope
Renowned teacher at Reims; promoted the abacus and Arabic numerals in the West
Previously abbot of Bobbio, archbishop of Reims and archbishop of Ravenna
Approved the archdioceses of Gniezno (1000) and Esztergom

faqs.question: Why is Sylvester II associated with mathematics?
faqs.answer: As Gerbert of Aurillac, he studied in Catalonia and became one of the first Western scholars to teach with Arabic numerals on the abacus, as well as astronomy with the astrolabe.

faqs.question: Was Pope Sylvester II accused of sorcery?
faqs.answer: Legends of magic surrounded him in later centuries, especially in twelfth-century chronicles. Historians regard them as fictions inspired by his unusual scientific learning.

faqs.question: What did Sylvester II do for Poland and Hungary?
faqs.answer: He approved new archdioceses at Gniezno and Esztergom, giving both nations their own church provinces, and tradition credits him with sending a crown to King Stephen of Hungary.

directAnswer: Pope John XVII reigned for less than six months in 1003, from May to November. Born John Sicco, he was chosen under the influence of the Roman patrician John Crescentius, and he is unusual in having been married with sons before entering the clergy.

paras: After Sylvester II's death in May 1003, power in Rome lay with John Crescentius, son of the Crescentius II executed in 1998. The new pope, John Sicco, was elected with his support. With no strong emperor present in Italy, the papacy once again depended on the Roman nobility.

sections.h2: A Pope Who Had Been Married
paras: The sources record that John Sicco had been married before his ordination and had three sons, all of whom became priests. In the early medieval Church, it was not unusual for a married man to be ordained after his wife's death or with her consent to separate, and this does not imply scandal.

John XVII died on 6 November 1003, after a pontificate of about six months. Few documents survive from his reign, and the Liber Pontificalis gives only basic information. He was buried in St. John Lateran.

keyFacts: Reigned 16 May 1003 to 6 November 1003
Born John Sicco in Rome
Elected under the influence of the patrician John Crescentius
Married with three sons, all priests, before ordination
Buried in St. John Lateran

faqs.question: Was Pope John XVII married?
faqs.answer: Yes, before entering the clergy. He had three sons, all of whom became priests.

faqs.question: Who controlled Rome during John XVII's reign?
faqs.answer: John Crescentius, a member of the powerful Crescentii family, held the dominant position in the city.

directAnswer: Pope John XVIII, born John Fasanus, reigned from Christmas 1003 to 1009. Elected under the influence of the Crescentii, he approved the new diocese of Bamberg at the request of King Henry II and ended his life as a monk at St. Paul Outside the Walls.

paras: John Fasanus was a Roman cleric, a cardinal-priest of St. Peter's at the time of his election. He took office on 25 December 1003, through the influence of the patrician John Crescentius. Although the emperors claimed authority over Rome, the city in his time remained under local noble control.

His most significant act came at the request of King Henry II of Germany. Henry wanted to found a new diocese at Bamberg, and in 1007 John approved it, placing it under special papal protection. Henry went on to make Bamberg a center of church life in his kingdom. John also confirmed privileges for monasteries and kept up correspondence with bishops north of the Alps.

Toward the end of his life, John left the papal office and became a monk at the monastery of St. Paul Outside the Walls, where he died. Historians generally believe he abdicated in 1009, although the exact circumstances are uncertain. He was buried at St. Paul's.

keyFacts: Reigned 25 December 1003 to 1009
Born John Fasanus in Rome
Elected with the support of the patrician John Crescentius
Approved the diocese of Bamberg for Henry II (1007)
Retired as a monk at St. Paul Outside the Walls

faqs.question: Why is John XVIII linked with Bamberg?
faqs.answer: He approved the founding of the diocese of Bamberg in 1007 at the request of King Henry II, who later became emperor.

faqs.question: Did John XVIII resign?
faqs.answer: He appears to have left office and become a monk at St. Paul Outside the Walls, where he died, though the exact details are unclear.

directAnswer: Pope Sergius IV, born Peter in Rome, reigned from 1009 to 1012. He was bishop of Albano before his election, served under the influence of the Crescentii, and was remembered for his care for the poor.

sections.h2: Peter 'Bucca Porci' and the Name Sergius
paras: Sergius was born in Rome, by some accounts the son of a shoemaker, and his own baptismal name was Peter. He was nicknamed Bucca Porci, often translated as 'pig's snout.' Some later tradition holds that he changed his name to avoid reigning as Peter II out of reverence for the apostle. Before his election he was bishop of Albano, near Rome, and some lists describe him as a Benedictine.

Sergius became pope on 31 July 1009, likely with the approval of John Crescentius. Despite that dependence, he is credited with relieving poverty in Rome during a period of famine, and his epitaph praises his generosity to the poor. He also granted privileges to monasteries and maintained cordial relations with Henry II of Germany.

In 1009 the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim ordered the destruction of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. A letter attributed to Sergius calls on Christians to free the holy places, but most historians doubt its authenticity and believe it may have been composed later, around the time of the First Crusade. Sergius died on 12 May 1012 and was buried in St. John Lateran.

keyFacts: Reigned 31 July 1009 to 12 May 1012
Born Peter in Rome; nicknamed Bucca Porci
Previously bishop of Albano
Remembered for aiding the poor during famine
A crusading letter in his name is of doubtful authenticity

faqs.question: What does 'Bucca Porci' mean?
faqs.answer: It is a Latin nickname usually translated as 'pig's snout.' It was attached to Sergius IV, whose original name was Peter.

faqs.question: Did Sergius IV call for a crusade?
faqs.answer: A letter attributed to him urges the liberation of the Holy Sepulchre after its destruction in 1009, but historians widely regard it as a later composition.

directAnswer: Pope Benedict VIII (reigned 1012–1024), born Theophylact of Tusculum, was the first of three popes from the Tusculan family. He crowned Henry II emperor in 1014, worked with him on church reform, and helped repel Saracen attacks on Italy's coast.

sections.h2: The Tusculan Family Takes the Papacy
paras: Theophylact was the son of Gregory, count of Tusculum, a family descended from the circle of Theophylact and Marozia that now challenged the Crescentii for control of Rome. In 1012, after the death of Sergius IV, the Tusculans secured his election. A rival faction elected a man named Gregory, now listed as an antipope, who fled to Germany seeking King Henry II's support.
Henry backed Benedict instead, and the alliance between the pope and the German king became the foundation of Benedict's reign. With Tusculan control of Rome, the Crescentii lost their dominance.

sections.h2: Henry II's Coronation and the Creed at Mass
paras: On 14 February 1014 Benedict crowned Henry II and his wife Cunigunde in St. Peter's. According to the abbot Berno of Reichenau, who was present, Henry asked that the Creed be sung at Mass in Rome, as was customary in Germany. Benedict agreed, and the Creed, including the Filioque phrase, became part of the Roman Mass from this time.
The Filioque had been accepted in Western theology for centuries, but its liturgical use at Rome later became one of the points of dispute between the Latin and Greek churches.

Benedict took an active role in defense. In 1016 Saracen forces under Mujahid, ruler of Denia, attacked the coast near Luni and occupied parts of Sardinia. The pope organized resistance and encouraged Pisa and Genoa to take action; their fleets drove the invaders from Sardinia.

In southern Italy he supported the Lombard noble Melus of Bari against Byzantine rule, but the rebellion was defeated at Cannae in 1018. Benedict then traveled to Bamberg in 1020 to persuade Henry II to intervene, and Henry issued a privilege confirming the papal possessions. The emperor led an expedition south in 1022.

In 1022 Benedict and Henry presided over a synod at Pavia that issued decrees against clerical marriage and concubinage, forbidding priests to live with women and declaring the children of clergy to be serfs of the Church. The measures aimed primarily to prevent the loss of church property and anticipated the broader reform movement of the later eleventh century.
Benedict died on 9 April 1024 and was succeeded by his brother Romanus, who became John XIX.

keyFacts: Reigned 18 May 1012 to 9 April 1024
Born Theophylact, son of Count Gregory of Tusculum
Crowned Henry II emperor on 14 February 1014
Allowed the Creed to be sung at the Roman Mass at Henry II's request
Encouraged Pisa and Genoa against Saracen forces in 1016
Presided with Henry II at the reforming Synod of Pavia (1022)

faqs.question: How did Benedict VIII change the Roman Mass?
faqs.answer: At Henry II's request in 1014, he allowed the Nicene Creed, with the Filioque, to be sung at Mass in Rome, following German practice.

faqs.question: What was Benedict VIII's relationship with Henry II?
faqs.answer: Henry supported Benedict against a rival claimant, and Benedict crowned him emperor in 1014. The two cooperated on church reform and Italian affairs.

faqs.question: What did the Synod of Pavia in 1022 decide?
faqs.answer: It forbade clerical marriage and concubinage and sought to protect church property from being passed to clergy's children.

directAnswer: Pope John XIX (reigned 1024–1032), born Romanus of Tusculum, succeeded his brother Benedict VIII while still a layman. He crowned Conrad II emperor in 1027 before King Cnut of England and invited the music teacher Guido of Arezzo to Rome to present his new system of notation.

sections.h2: From Consul and Senator to Pope
paras: Romanus, a son of Count Gregory of Tusculum, held the civil leadership of Rome during his brother's pontificate, with titles such as consul and senator. When Benedict VIII died in April 1024, Romanus was elected to succeed him. Because he was a layman, he received all the clerical orders in rapid succession. Contemporary writers criticized the election as a family arrangement secured through influence and money.

The succession kept the papacy firmly in Tusculan hands. Another brother, Alberic III, held the leading position among the family's lay members, and it was his son who would follow John on the papal throne. For eight years the city's civil and spiritual leadership were again concentrated in a single household.

The Burgundian chronicler Rodulfus Glaber reports that in 1024 envoys of the Byzantine emperor and Patriarch Eustathius asked John to recognize the patriarch of Constantinople as universal within his own sphere, offering generous gifts. According to Glaber, protests from Western churchmen and monks led John to drop the proposal. The episode is known only from Glaber and some related sources, so details remain uncertain.

On Easter Day, 26 March 1027, John crowned Conrad II emperor and his wife Gisela empress in St. Peter's. The ceremony was attended by King Cnut of England and Denmark and King Rudolph III of Burgundy. Cnut later wrote that he used the visit to obtain reduced fees for English archbishops receiving the pallium and protection for English pilgrims traveling to Rome.
John's cooperation with Conrad continued in other matters, including disputes between the patriarchates of Aquileia and Grado, in which papal decisions shifted with the political situation.

sections.h2: Guido of Arezzo and Musical Notation
paras: Around 1028 John invited Guido of Arezzo, a Benedictine music teacher, to Rome. Guido had developed a system of lines and spaces that let singers learn chant much faster than by memory alone. According to Guido's own letter, the pope examined his antiphonary and was able to sing a melody he had never heard before. John's endorsement helped the new method gain acceptance.
John XIX died in October 1032. His nephew Theophylact succeeded him as Benedict IX.

keyFacts: Reigned 9 April 1024 to 20 October 1032
Born Romanus, brother of Benedict VIII; a layman when elected
Crowned Conrad II emperor on Easter 1027, with Cnut present
Cnut secured lower pallium fees for English archbishops
Invited Guido of Arezzo to Rome and endorsed his musical notation

faqs.question: Why was John XIX's election criticized?
faqs.answer: He was a layman from the ruling Tusculan family who succeeded his own brother, and contemporaries believed influence and money secured his election.

faqs.question: How did John XIX support Guido of Arezzo?
faqs.answer: He brought Guido to Rome around 1028 and examined his new notation system. Guido reported that the pope sang an unfamiliar melody at sight using it.

faqs.question: Which kings attended Conrad II's coronation by John XIX?
faqs.answer: King Cnut of England and Denmark and King Rudolph III of Burgundy attended the Easter 1027 coronation.

directAnswer: Pope Benedict IX, born Theophylact of Tusculum, first became pope in 1032 as the nephew of his two predecessors and is often described as the youngest pope in history. He is the only man to have held the papacy on three separate occasions; this first term lasted until a Roman revolt in 1044–1045.

paras: Theophylact was a son of Alberic III, count of Tusculum, and the nephew of Benedict VIII and John XIX. After his uncle John's death in 1032, the family secured his election. He took the name Benedict, as his uncle Theophylact had done before him.

His age at election is uncertain. Rodulfus Glaber claimed he was a boy of about ten or twelve, but modern historians consider that an exaggeration and think he was more likely in his late teens or around twenty. Even so, he is usually counted as the youngest person ever to hold the office.

Despite his reputation, Benedict's first years included routine church business. He met Emperor Conrad II at Cremona in 1037 and, at Conrad's request, excommunicated Archbishop Aribert of Milan, who had revolted against the emperor. He canonized Simeon of Trier, a hermit who had lived in the Porta Nigra, and granted privileges to monasteries.

However, his personal conduct drew severe condemnation from later reformers. Writers such as Peter Damian and the author of the work attributed to Pope Victor III described his life in harsh terms. Some of their accusations are hard to verify, but there is little doubt that his reign was regarded even at the time as a low point.

By the 1040s opposition among Roman nobles, including rival families such as the Crescentii, was growing. In September 1044 a revolt drove Benedict from Rome. In January 1045 the Romans elected John, bishop of Sabina, as Sylvester III. Benedict's family kept its strongholds outside the city, and within weeks he was able to return and expel his rival.
The events of 1044–1045 opened a period of confusion that would see Benedict hold the papacy twice more and that ultimately led to King Henry III's intervention at the Council of Sutri in 1046.

Benedict's turbulent career became one of the arguments used by eleventh-century reformers for freeing papal elections from the control of Roman families. The reform movement that followed, culminating in the 1059 decree assigning election to the cardinals, was shaped in part by the memory of his pontificates.

keyFacts: First reign: 21 October 1032 to 13 January 1045
Born Theophylact, son of Alberic III of Tusculum
Nephew of Benedict VIII and John XIX
Often described as the youngest pope; exact age uncertain
Excommunicated Aribert of Milan at Conrad II's request (1038)
The only man to hold the papacy three separate times

faqs.question: How old was Benedict IX when he became pope?
faqs.answer: Sources disagree. One chronicler claimed he was about ten or twelve, but historians think he was more likely around eighteen to twenty.

faqs.question: Why did Benedict IX's first reign end?
faqs.answer: A revolt of Roman nobles in 1044 forced him out of the city, and in January 1045 the Romans elected Sylvester III in his place.

faqs.question: Did Benedict IX perform any normal papal acts?
faqs.answer: Yes. He canonized Simeon of Trier, granted monastic privileges, and cooperated with Emperor Conrad II on Italian affairs.

directAnswer: Pope Sylvester III, previously John, bishop of Sabina, was elected in January 1045 after a revolt drove Benedict IX from Rome. He held the city only until March or April 1045, and in 1046 the Council of Sutri deposed him, though the Church still lists him among the popes.

sections.h2: The Bishop of Sabina Is Elected
paras: John was bishop of Sabina, a diocese northeast of Rome. When Roman nobles, probably with the support of the Crescentii family, drove Benedict IX out of the city in 1044, they elected John in January 1045. He took the name Sylvester.

Benedict's family remained powerful outside Rome. By March 1045 Benedict had returned and forced Sylvester out. Sylvester went back to his diocese of Sabina. Because his election occurred while Benedict had not resigned, its validity was questioned then and later.

In December 1046 King Henry III convened a council at Sutri to settle the competing claims to the papacy. The council deposed Sylvester and sentenced him to confinement in a monastery. In practice he seems to have returned to his role as bishop of Sabina, where he appears in records for years afterward, until about 1062. The Vatican's official list includes him, while noting the uncertainty around his status.

keyFacts: Reigned 16 January 1045 to 10 April 1045 (per the official list)
Previously John, bishop of Sabina
Elected after a Roman revolt expelled Benedict IX
Driven out when Benedict returned
Deposed at the Council of Sutri in 1046

faqs.question: Why is Sylvester III's legitimacy questioned?
faqs.answer: He was elected while Benedict IX had not resigned, so many contemporaries and later historians doubted the validity of his election.

faqs.question: What happened to Sylvester III after his deposition?
faqs.answer: The Council of Sutri ordered him confined to a monastery, but records suggest he continued as bishop of Sabina for years.

directAnswer: Benedict IX's second term as pope lasted only a few weeks in the spring of 1045, after he drove out Sylvester III. It ended on 1 May 1045, when he resigned the papacy in favor of his godfather, the archpriest John Gratian, in exchange for a payment.

paras: After Roman nobles elected Sylvester III in January 1045, Benedict IX used his family's strongholds outside the city to organize a return. By March or April he had re-entered Rome and forced Sylvester back to his diocese of Sabina. The official papal list counts this as Benedict's second pontificate, beginning on 10 April 1045.

Benedict did not hold power long. On 1 May 1045 he resigned in favor of his godfather, John Gratian, archpriest of the church of St. John at the Latin Gate, who paid him a large sum. Accounts differ on the reasons. Some sources say Benedict wished to marry; others suggest he wanted a secure income after giving up a difficult position.

John Gratian, who became Gregory VI, may have acted out of a sincere wish to free the Church from an unworthy pope. But the transaction was widely regarded as simony, and it set the stage for Henry III's intervention.

Benedict did not fully accept his own resignation. Soon there were three rival claims: his own, Sylvester III's, and Gregory VI's. Henry III's council at Sutri in December 1046, followed by a synod at Rome, declared all three deposed or removed.

keyFacts: Second reign: 10 April 1045 to 1 May 1045
Returned to Rome by expelling Sylvester III
Resigned in favor of his godfather John Gratian (Gregory VI)
Received a payment for resigning, later condemned as simony
Deposed by the Council of Sutri and a Roman synod in 1046

faqs.question: Did Benedict IX sell the papacy?
faqs.answer: He resigned in May 1045 in favor of his godfather John Gratian, who paid him a large sum. The arrangement was condemned as simony.

faqs.question: Why did Benedict IX resign in 1045?
faqs.answer: Sources disagree. Some say he hoped to marry, while others suggest he simply wanted a secure income after giving up office.

directAnswer: Pope Gregory VI, born John Gratian, was a respected Roman archpriest who became pope in May 1045 after paying Benedict IX to resign. Though welcomed by reformers, he was removed at the Council of Sutri in 1046 for simony and died in exile in Germany, accompanied by the future Pope Gregory VII.

sections.h2: John Gratian, Archpriest of St. John at the Latin Gate
paras: John Gratian was archpriest of the church of St. John at the Latin Gate in Rome and was Benedict IX's godfather. He was known for his piety and learning. When Benedict was willing to resign, John Gratian paid him a large sum to step aside and was installed as pope on 1 May 1045, taking the name Gregory.
Reform-minded churchmen were at first delighted. St. Peter Damian wrote to the new pope, welcoming him as a restorer of the Church's dignity after the turmoil of Benedict's reign.

sections.h2: A Reform-Minded Pope with a Tainted Title
paras: Gregory's motives appear to have been sincere: he seems to have wanted to free the Church from a pope widely seen as unworthy. But the payment was hard to distinguish from simony. As Benedict IX and Sylvester III continued to press their own claims, Rome had three rival popes, and Gregory was unable to secure control of the city or its revenues.

King Henry III of Germany came to Italy in 1046, intending to be crowned emperor and determined to end the confusion. He convened a council at Sutri on 20 December 1046. Gregory presided at first, but when the facts of his election were examined, he either resigned or was deposed; the sources give different accounts. A few days later Henry's candidate, Suidger of Bamberg, was elected as Clement II.

Sutri showed that a German king could settle a disputed papacy by his own authority. Reformers welcomed the result, which ended the scandal of rival claimants, but later generations grew uneasy with the precedent of royal control over who sat in the chair of Peter.

Gregory was sent into exile in Germany, where he died in 1047 or 1048, probably near Cologne. A young Roman cleric named Hildebrand, his chaplain, accompanied him. Hildebrand returned to Rome with Leo IX and later became pope himself in 1073. Many historians think his choice of the name Gregory VII was a tribute to his old patron, implying that he regarded Gregory VI as a legitimate pope.

keyFacts: Reigned 1 May 1045 to 20 December 1046
Born John Gratian; archpriest of St. John at the Latin Gate
Godfather of Benedict IX, whom he paid to resign
Removed at the Council of Sutri under Henry III
Died in exile in Germany; accompanied by Hildebrand, the future Gregory VII

faqs.question: Why was Gregory VI removed?
faqs.answer: He had paid Benedict IX to resign. Though his motives may have been good, the Council of Sutri treated the payment as simony.

faqs.question: How is Gregory VI connected to Gregory VII?
faqs.answer: Hildebrand, later Gregory VII, served as his chaplain and followed him into exile. Many historians believe his papal name honored Gregory VI.

faqs.question: What did reformers think of Gregory VI?
faqs.answer: Many welcomed him at first. St. Peter Damian wrote to congratulate him, hoping he would restore order to the Church.

directAnswer: Pope Clement II (reigned 1046–1047), born Suidger, was the bishop of Bamberg chosen by King Henry III at the Council of Sutri. On the day of his consecration, Christmas 1046, he crowned Henry emperor. He held a synod against simony, died within ten months, and is the only pope buried north of the Alps.

sections.h2: Suidger, Saxon Noble and Bishop of Bamberg
paras: Suidger was born into a noble Saxon family, traditionally associated with Hornburg in Saxony. He served as a canon at Halberstadt and in the royal chapel before Henry III appointed him bishop of Bamberg in 1040. He accompanied Henry on his journey to Italy in 1046.

sections.h2: Elected at Sutri, Consecrated at Christmas
paras: After the Council of Sutri removed Gregory VI, and Benedict IX and Sylvester III were set aside, Henry III proposed Suidger as pope. The Roman clergy and people accepted him, and he took the name Clement. He was consecrated on Christmas Day 1046, and on the same day he crowned Henry III and Queen Agnes as emperor and empress.
Clement kept his bishopric of Bamberg, a sign of his close attachment to the German church and to Henry's circle.

In January 1047 Clement held a synod in Rome that condemned simony and imposed penalties on those who had knowingly received ordination from simoniac bishops. The decrees signaled the beginning of a period of German reforming popes who would transform the papacy over the following decades. Clement also canonized Wiborada, a recluse of St. Gall killed during a Magyar raid in 926.

He was the first of a line of popes from the German lands chosen with Henry III's backing, followed by Damasus II, Leo IX and Victor II. Together they turned the papacy from a prize of Roman families into the driving force of church reform.

sections.h2: Death and a Grave in Bamberg
paras: Clement died on 9 October 1047 at the monastery of San Tommaso near Pesaro, after less than a year in office. His body was taken to Bamberg and buried in the cathedral, making him the only pope buried in Germany, indeed north of the Alps.

Rumors that he had been poisoned circulated at the time. A twentieth-century examination of his remains reportedly found high levels of lead, which some have read as support for poisoning, though the evidence is not conclusive. After his death, Benedict IX returned to Rome for a third time.

keyFacts: Reigned 20 December 1046 to 9 October 1047
Born Suidger, a Saxon noble; bishop of Bamberg from 1040
Chosen by Henry III at the Council of Sutri
Crowned Henry III emperor on Christmas Day 1046
Held a synod against simony in January 1047
Buried in Bamberg Cathedral, the only papal tomb north of the Alps

faqs.question: Where is Pope Clement II buried?
faqs.answer: He is buried in Bamberg Cathedral in Germany, the only pope whose tomb lies north of the Alps.

faqs.question: Was Clement II poisoned?
faqs.answer: Contemporaries suspected it, and a twentieth-century study of his remains reportedly found high lead levels, but the cause of his death cannot be established with certainty.

faqs.question: Why did Clement II keep his bishopric of Bamberg?
faqs.answer: He remained deeply tied to the German church and Henry III's court, and he retained Bamberg alongside the papacy for his short reign.

directAnswer: Benedict IX's third and final term as pope began after Clement II's death in October 1047 and ended in July 1048, when Margrave Boniface of Tuscany, acting for Emperor Henry III, drove him from Rome. He made no further successful claim to the papacy and died around 1055 or 1056.

sections.h2: Seizing the Opportunity of Clement II's Death
paras: When Clement II died unexpectedly in October 1047, Benedict IX, who had never accepted his removal at Sutri, moved quickly. With the support of his family and allies in Rome, he regained control of the Lateran. The official list dates this third pontificate from 9 October 1047.

Henry III did not accept Benedict's return. He nominated Poppo, bishop of Brixen, as pope and ordered Boniface, margrave of Tuscany, to install him. Boniface at first hesitated, but under the emperor's pressure he marched on Rome, and Benedict was driven out in July 1048. Poppo became Damasus II, though he died within weeks.

Benedict was afterward excommunicated, and he never again held Rome. The details of his last years are thin. A tradition associated with the abbey of Grottaferrata, near Tusculum, holds that he ended his life there in penance, and he probably died around 1055 or 1056. His three reigns remain a unique and cautionary episode in papal history.

keyFacts: Third reign: 9 October 1047 to 17 July 1048
Returned to power after the death of Clement II
Expelled by Margrave Boniface of Tuscany on Henry III's orders
Succeeded by Damasus II (Poppo of Brixen)
Later excommunicated; died c. 1055–1056

faqs.question: How did Benedict IX's third pontificate end?
faqs.answer: Emperor Henry III ordered Margrave Boniface of Tuscany to remove him, and Boniface expelled him from Rome in July 1048.

faqs.question: Did Benedict IX repent?
faqs.answer: A tradition linked to the abbey of Grottaferrata holds that he died there as a penitent, but this cannot be confirmed from contemporary sources.
